title.en: The Wheel of Life: Buddha's Pictorial Universe

region.en: Doorways of Tibetan temples, where the Wheel is painted (symbolic pin at Samye)
region.zh: 藏地寺門所繪之輪（以桑耶寺為象徵定位）

texts.period: Pictorial Wheel of Life (Bhavacakra); Tibetan copy attributed to the Indian monk Bande Yeshe, 8th century; Waddell 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. on Metaphysics

summary.en: The Tibetan Wheel of Life is a disc symbolizing the endless cycle of existence, of which each rebirth is a revolution, held in the clutches of a monster who represents the hideousness of the Clinging to Life; the broad tire is occupied by the Causal Nexus, and the nave by the three vices - the Daughters of Desire, Raga, Dvesa, Moha, lust, ill-will and stupidity - figured as a dove, serpent and pig; outside the wheel is a figure of Buddha, showing that he has escaped from the cycle, pointing the way of escape. The six regions of rebirth - gods, Titans, men, beasts, tantalized ghosts and hell - are shown in the middle whorl, demarcated by rainbow-coloured cordons, and the twelve links round the rim follow the chain of causation from Unconscious Will to Decay and Death.
summary.zh: 藏式生命之輪是一圓盤，象徵生死無盡的輪迴——每一次轉生即一週轉；輪為怪獸利爪所攫，喻「戀生」之可怖；輪輞為十二因緣，輪轂為三毒——貪、瞋、癡，即「欲之三女」，畫作鴿、蛇、豬；輪外立佛像，示其已出離此輪，並指解脫之道。中輪畫六道——天、非天（阿修羅）、人、畜、餓鬼、地獄——以虹色界線相隔，而輪輞十二環節由「無明」至「老死」次第相續。

sensitivity.note: Living iconographic tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: The Tibetan form of the picture should be studied with its Key; it is a disc or wheel, symbolizing the endless cycle of Life, of which each re-birth is a revolution. The wheel is held in the clutches of a monster, who represents the hideousness of the Clinging to Life; the broad tire is occupied by the Causal Nexus, and the nave by the three vices or delusions, the Daughters of Desire - lust, ill-will, stupidity - which lie at the core of re-birth, and are figured here as a dove, serpent and pig, appropriately coloured red, green and black; while outside the wheel is a figure of Buddha, showing that he has escaped from the cycle, to which he is represented as pointing the way of escape.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The various regions of re-birth, the Gati, are pictorially represented in the drawing called The Wheel of Life; they are given as six, and are thus enumerated in the order of their superiority: the Gods, the Titans, Man, the Beasts, the Tantalized Ghosts, and Hell. Existence in the first three worlds is considered superior or good, and in the last three inferior or bad; the six regions of re-birth are shown in the middle whorl, demarcated from each other by rainbow-coloured cordons representing the atmospheric zones that separate the different worlds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the picture the phases of life are depicted: birth in a cottage; children at play; village scenes with people drinking wine under the shade of a tree; labour by sweat of brow; a man and horse falling into a river; two men fighting, one under trial before the judge; the king and his ministers; decrepit old people; a physician feeling the pulse of a patient; a corpse with a Lama feeling whether breath be extinct and relatives weeping; and funeral ceremonies, a corpse being carried off to the funeral pyre on the top of a hill preceded by a Lama blowing a thigh-bone trumpet and rattling a hand-drum - he also has hold of the end of a white scarf affixed to the corpse, the object of which is to guide the soul by the white path to the pyre so that it may be disposed of in the orthodox manner, have the best chance of a good re-birth, and may not stray and get caught by outside demons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: The Twelve Nidanas: Buddha's Chain of Causation

region.en: Under the Tree of Wisdom at Gaya (symbolic pin at Bodh Gaya)
region.zh: 菩提伽耶智慧樹下（以菩提伽耶為象徵定位）

texts.period: Chain of Causation formulated by the Buddha; Tibetan picture attributed to Bande Yeshe, 8th century; Waddell 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. on Metaphysics

summary.en: Buddha formulated his view of life into a twelve-linked closed chain called the Wheel of Life or of 'Becoming', or the Causal Nexus, which he is represented in the Vinaya scripture itself to have thought out under the Tree of Wisdom; the way in which the narrative is couched leads to the impression that it was precisely the insight into this Wheel of Life which constituted his Buddhahood and distinguished him from the other Arhats. The twelve links round the rim follow in evolutionary fashion: Unconscious Will (Avidya), Conformations (Samskara), Consciousness (Vijnana), Self-consciousness (Nama-rupa), Sense-surfaces and Understanding (Shadayatana), Contact (Sparsha), Feeling (Vedana), Desire (Trishna), Indulgence (Upadana), Fuller Life (Bhava), Birth of heir (Jati), Decay and Death (Jaramarana) - and passing from Death to Re-birth, the chain closes back on Unconscious Will.
summary.zh: 佛陀將其人生觀結為十二環節之封閉鎖鏈——「有輪」或「緣起」；經藏中言其於智慧樹下思得此輪——敘事之筆，令人覺得正是洞見此「生命之輪」，方成其佛覺，而異於其他阿羅漢。輪輞十二環節次第為：無明、行、識、名色、六入、觸、受、愛、取、有、生、老死——而由死轉生，復歸無明，閉環不已。

sensitivity.note: Living doctrinal tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Buddha formulated his view of life into a twelve-linked closed chain called the Wheel of Life or of Becoming, or the Causal Nexus; which he is represented, in the Vinaya scripture itself, to have thought out under the Tree of Wisdom. The way in which the narrative is couched leads, indeed, to the impression that it was precisely the insight into this Wheel of Life which constituted his Buddhahood, and distinguished him from the other Arhats; he gave it a very leading place in his philosophy, so that the stanza recounting its utterance - Of all objects which proceed from a Cause, the Tathagatha has explained the cause, and he has explained their cessation also; this is the doctrine of the great Samana - is the most frequent of all Buddhist inscriptions.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The introduction of the pictorial details is ascribed to the great Indian monk Nagarjuna, who lived in the second century AD; these pictorial details, however, are alleged to be objective representations of the self-same similes used by Buddha himself, who constantly used homely similes and allegories to illustrate his doctrines. The Tibetan picture which supplements the Ajanta painting is alleged to be a copy of one brought to Tibet by the Indian monk Bande Yeshe in the eighth century AD, and now at Sam-yas monastery.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: The Jataka Tales and the Wheel of Karma

region.en: The 550 births of the Buddha (symbolic pin at the Indian mission fields)
region.zh: 佛陀五百五十生（以印度傳教場域為象徵定位）

texts.period: Jataka tradition (Buddha's births numbered at 550); Waddell 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. on Karma and Palingenesis

summary.en: In this way Buddha explained all the acts and events of his life, his joys and sorrows, his success and failures, his virtues and weaknesses, as results of things done by him in previous states of life, which he recalled to mind as occasion arose for teaching purposes; and thus those anecdotes of the antecedent lives of the Buddha - the so-called Jataka tales - with the moral lessons derived from them, came to be among the most cherished items of Buddhist belief. Buddha's births are usually numbered at 550, of which the latter and more important are called 'the Great Births'.
summary.zh: 佛陀如是解說自己一生的一切行止與際遇——其樂與憂、其成與敗、其德與弱——皆是宿世所作之果；每當教化之需，他便憶念宣說。由此，佛陀前世之軼事——所謂「本生譚」——及其道德教訓，遂成為佛教信仰中最受珍視的篇章。佛陀之生通常計為五百五十，其中後期而重要者稱「大生」。

sensitivity.note: Living narrative tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: In this way Buddha explained all the acts and events of his life, his joys and sorrows, his success and failures, his virtues and weaknesses, as results of things done by him in previous states of life, which he recalled to mind as occasion arose for teaching purposes; and thus those anecdotes of the antecedent lives of the Buddha - the so-called Jataka tales - with the moral lessons derived from them, came to be among the most cherished items of Buddhist belief. Buddha's births are usually numbered at 550, of which the latter and more important are called the Great Births.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
